extracted.intended_audience: NIH extramural applicants / principal investigators / grant writers preparing resubmissions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and practical commentary on preparing NIH resubmission (amended) grant applications, especially what to put in the one-page Introduction and how to (not) mark changes per recent NIH notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission allowance and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: It is permitted to resubmit a previously unfunded NIH grant application. At present time, one is allowed a single amended version which goes in at a different receipt date (typically one month later than new proposals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resubmissions are limited to one amended version; plan timing accordingly (different receipt date, often ~1 month after a new submission deadline). Historical practice allowed more amendments but current NIH policy limits applicants to a single resubmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction: must respond to prior critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: The Introduction to the Resubmitted grant is supposed to respond to the critiques supplied in review of the original version, and part of the review is supposed to cover how well the PI has responded to the prior criticisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Introduction to directly address reviewer criticisms from the Summary Statement. Reviewers are expected to evaluate how thoroughly and effectively the PI has addressed prior critiques; therefore prioritize clear, specific responses to each major weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction must include summary of substantial additions, deletions, and changes and response to weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Introduction must include a summary of substantial additions, deletions, and changes to the application. It must also include a response to weaknesses raised in the Summary Statement.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This NIH instruction requires both (a) a concise summary of what was changed in the application and (b) direct responses to weaknesses noted previously. Fit both demands into the allowed Introduction space (see page limit). Be explicit about what was added, removed, or revised and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction length/page limit
rubrics_metrics.description: At present ... the amended version ... can include a one page Introduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Introduction to a resubmission is generally limited to one page (historically it was longer). Given the tight space, be concise and prioritize the most important changes and responses to critical reviewer concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on using markup to identify changes (NOT-OD-24-061)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective May 25, 2024, this guidance replaces previous guidance on marking changes in Resubmission applications. The use of markups such as bracketing, indenting, highlighting, bolding, italicizing, underlining, margin lines, change in typography, font, or font color, or any other type of markup should not be used to identify changes in Resubmission applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mark up the application text/figures to show changes (no brackets, lines, font/color changes, bold/italic emphasis, highlighting, etc.). This NOT replaces/supersedes prior notices and rescinds the 2014 notice; interpret 'should not' in this context as a prohibition. Be aware that enforcement may vary and that earlier common practices (margin lines, bolding) are now disallowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Previously accepted methods for indicating changes (historical practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common older methods to indicate changes included left margin lines, bold or italics text, and sometimes indenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though these methods were commonly used (and were once expected by reviewers), they are now specifically listed among markups that should not be used. Do not rely on historical practices when preparing current resubmissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of uneven reviewer expectations/enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Uneven application of these rules by reviewers can disadvantage applicants: if you refrain from marking changes while others do, you may be at a disadvantage because many reviewers expect to see changes indicated; conversely, some reviewers may penalize applicants who indicate changes despite policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the practical risk that reviewers' expectations vary. Consider mitigation strategies (see next metric). Document your choices clearly in the Introduction so reviewers understand your compliance with NIH policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended practice: include statement that changes are not marked per current NIH policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The author reports: 'I have taken to including a statement in my Introductions that changes are not marked per “current NIH policy” to deal with this situation as best I can.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including an explicit sentence in the Introduction that you have not marked changes because of NIH policy can reduce reviewer confusion and explain why they will not see brackets or margin lines. This is a pragmatic workaround to uneven reviewer expectations, but does not substitute for clear, specific responses to prior critiques.
